Child care expense deduction: the three limits, why the lower-income spouse claims, and how the same deduction raises the Canada child benefit

Work out the 2025 child care expense deduction on line 21400 from the per-child limits, two-thirds of the claimant’s earned income and what was actually paid, then add the two things it is worth: income tax saved and a larger Canada child benefit for July 2026 to June 2027. Includes how the value changes with family income and what full-time child care costs according to Statistics Canada.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 8 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Child care expense deduction (line 21400) for 2025: the three limits, which spouse claims, the tax it saves and the larger Canada child benefit from July 2026

Interactive planning lab

Child care expense deduction allowed for 2025 (line 21400)$12,000
Per-child limits added together$13,000
Two-thirds of the claimant’s earned income$20,000
Income tax saved at the assumed rate$2,346
Extra Canada child benefit, July 2026 to June 2027$684
Tax saved and extra CCB together$3,030
Child care paid, less the tax saved and extra CCB$8,970
Share of child care paid that comes back25.25%

With 1 child under 7 and 1 aged 7 to 16, $12,000 of 2025 child care and $30,000 of earned income for the lower-income spouse, the deduction is $12,000, set by the expenses paid. The lower-income spouse claims, as CRA requires. At the assumed 19.55% marginal rate it saves $2,346.00 of income tax. It also lowers adjusted family net income from $100,000 to $88,000, which raises the July 2026 to June 2027 Canada child benefit from $8,040.28 to $8,724.28, $684.00 more. Together $3,030.00 comes back, 25.3% of what was paid. The tax rate is an assumption; provincial child care credits (such as Ontario’s CARE credit), the child disability benefit, GST/HST credit and other income-tested amounts are not included.

The central idea

For 2025, the child care expense deduction is the least of three amounts: eligible expenses paid, CAD 8,000 per child under 7 at year end plus CAD 5,000 per child aged 7 to 16 (CAD 11,000 for a child eligible for the disability tax credit), and two-thirds of the claimant’s earned income. In a couple, the spouse with the lower net income must claim it, except in a few listed situations. Because it is a deduction, it also lowers adjusted family net income, so the Canada child benefit for July 2026 to June 2027 rises by the CCB reduction rate times the deduction: 7%, 13.5%, 19% or 23% in the first band for one to four or more children, and 3.2% to 9.5% above CAD 82,847. In the default example, CAD 12,000 of care for two children comes back as about CAD 2,346 of tax and CAD 684 of CCB, about a quarter of the cost.

01

One deduction, two returns

Parents who pay for child care so they can work can deduct part of it on line 21400 of their return. Most of the attention goes to the tax saving. But because it is a deduction rather than a credit, it also lowers net income, and adjusted family net income is what sets the Canada child benefit. A 2025 deduction therefore pays twice: once as a lower 2025 tax bill, and again as higher CCB payments from July 2026 to June 2027.

The calculator works out the deduction from CRA’s three limits, applies an editable tax rate to estimate the tax saved, and recomputes the CCB with and without the deduction. Its default is a couple with one child under 6 and one aged 7 to 16, CAD 12,000 of care paid for 2025, and net incomes of CAD 30,000 and CAD 70,000.

02

The three limits

CRA’s Income Tax Folio S1-F3-C1 (¶1.38.1 to ¶1.41) sets the deduction for a year at the least of:

LimitAmount
Eligible child care expenses paid for services in the yearWhat you actually paid, with receipts
The annual child care expense amount, added up over the childrenCAD 8,000 per child under 7 at the end of the year; CAD 5,000 per child aged 7 to 16, or older with a mental or physical infirmity; CAD 11,000 per child eligible for the disability tax credit
Two-thirds of the claimant’s earned incomeMainly employment income and net self-employment income from active work, plus CPP or QPP disability benefits and some grants and awards

The per-child amounts are pooled: a family with one child under 7 and one aged 9 has a combined limit of CAD 13,000, and can use it even if most of the cost is for the younger child. Expenses above the limits are simply lost; CRA’s how-to-claim page says unclaimed expenses cannot be carried forward. Eligible expenses include daycare, nursery school, day camps and day sports schools, and boarding schools and overnight camps up to a weekly amount; the care must let a parent work, run a business, study or do research, and payments to the child’s other parent or to a relative under 18 do not count.

03

Why the lower-income spouse claims

CRA’s page on who can claim is direct: the person with the lower net income, including zero income, must claim. If incomes are equal, the couple agree which of them claims. The higher-income spouse can claim only for the period in which the lower-income spouse was a student in a qualifying program, unable to care for children because of an infirmity or a hospital stay of two weeks or more (with a doctor’s statement), in prison for two weeks or more, or separated because of a breakdown in the relationship. Even then the claim is limited per week: the folio’s periodic amount is 1/40 of the annual amount, which works out to CAD 200, CAD 125 or CAD 275 a week per child.

The rule has two consequences that surprise families. First, the claim usually goes to the spouse in the lower tax bracket, so the tax saving is smaller than if the higher earner could claim. Second, a lower earner with little earned income hits the two-thirds limit: CAD 15,000 of earnings supports at most CAD 10,000 of deduction, whatever was paid.

04

How the deduction feeds the CCB

CRA’s CCB calculation for July 2026 to June 2027 uses 2025 adjusted family net income: the two spouses’ net incomes after deductions such as this one. The maximum is CAD 8,157 a year per child under 6 and CAD 6,883 per child aged 6 to 17. It is reduced as follows:

ChildrenIncome CAD 38,237 to 82,847Above CAD 82,847
17% of income over CAD 38,237CAD 3,123 + 3.2% of income over CAD 82,847
213.5%CAD 6,022 + 5.7%
319%CAD 8,476 + 8%
4 or more23%CAD 10,260 + 9.5%

So as long as the family stays within one band and still gets some CCB, each dollar of deduction adds the band’s rate to the benefit. In the default case, CAD 12,000 of deduction at CAD 100,000 of family income adds 5.7% × CAD 12,000 = CAD 684, about CAD 57 a month. For a family with two children and income in the first band the same deduction adds CAD 1,620. Below CAD 38,237 the full benefit is already paid and the deduction adds nothing to it. The age bands differ from the deduction’s: a child who was 6 at the end of 2025 counts towards the CAD 8,000 limit but receives the 6-to-17 CCB amount, which is why the calculator asks separately how many children are under 6.

05

Five worked cases

Each case uses a 19.55% marginal rate (the 2025 federal lowest rate of 14.5% plus Ontario’s 5.05%) and CAD 16,129 of tax-free income for the claimant, both editable.

In the second case the family’s income falls from CAD 85,000 to CAD 75,000, crossing back into the 13.5% band, which is why the CCB gain is larger than 5.7% of CAD 10,000. In the third, the deduction takes family income from CAD 50,000 to CAD 38,000, below the first threshold, so only CAD 11,763 of it earns the 13.5% rate. An independent 40-digit decimal check reproduces every figure in the table.

06

What full-time child care costs, by Statistics Canada’s measure

Statistics Canada reported in October 2025 that parents of children aged 0 to 5 in full-time centre-based care (30 hours or more a week) paid a mean of CAD 435 a month in 2025, down from CAD 663 in 2022 (the 2022 figure excludes the territories, and the survey sources differ). Provincial means ranged from CAD 206 in Prince Edward Island to CAD 571 in British Columbia. Multiplied by 12, even British Columbia’s mean is about CAD 6,852 a year, below the CAD 8,000 limit for one child under 7.

For a young child in a regulated full-time space, then, the amount paid is often what sets the deduction. The limits matter more for unregulated or private care, for nannies, and for school-age children whose before- and after-school care and summer day camps can exceed CAD 5,000. These are means of what parents reported, not the price of any particular space; your own receipts decide the claim.

07

Claiming it and planning around it

  1. Collect receipts with the provider’s details. CRA requires a receipt for each payment; an individual provider’s receipt must show their social insurance number. Keep them if you file online.
  2. Use Form T778. Form T778 Parts A and B work out the deduction; Part C is only for a higher-income spouse in one of the listed situations, Part D for a claimant who was a student.
  3. Check which limit binds. If two-thirds of the lower earner’s earned income binds, extra paid care gives no deduction. If the per-child limits bind, it does not matter which child the care was for.
  4. File both returns on time. The CCB for July 2026 depends on both spouses having filed for 2025; a deduction claimed late is reassessed, and CRA recalculates the benefit.
  5. Look at the other deductions. RRSP, FHSA and union dues also reduce family net income. A household inside a CCB reduction band gets the band’s rate on top of the tax saving from any of them.

08

What the calculator leaves out

  • The exact tax. The tax saved is the deduction above the tax-free level times an editable rate. It ignores brackets the deduction may cross, other credits, and provincial reductions.
  • Provincial programs. Ontario’s CARE credit and Quebec’s refundable child care credit, which replaces the deduction in Quebec for provincial tax, are not modelled, nor are provincial child benefits.
  • Other income-tested amounts. The GST/HST credit, Canada workers benefit and child disability benefit also depend on family net income and can rise too.
  • Special situations. Single parents, the higher-income spouse’s weekly claims, students, boarding schools and overnight camps, and children eligible for the disability tax credit are described but not modelled.
  • Benefit-year changes. Children’s birthdays during July 2026 to June 2027, shared custody, and changes in marital status change the CCB month by month.
  • Years. Only the 2025 deduction and the July 2026 to June 2027 CCB amounts are used.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 27 October 2026. The fifth chart uses Statistics Canada’s parent-reported mean monthly expense for children aged 0 to 5 in full-time centre-based care (The Daily, released 21 October 2025), an observation; multiplying it by 12 is a calculation. The other four apply CRA’s Income Tax Folio S1-F3-C1 (effective 9 December 2024), CRA’s line 21400 pages (page details 20 January 2026) and CRA’s Canada child benefit calculation for July 2026 to June 2027 (page details 22 October 2026), reviewed 27 October 2026, to hypothetical editable households: a two-parent family with children under 18, all of whom qualify for the CCB. The income tax saved uses an editable marginal rate and tax-free level, not a full tax calculation. Provincial child care credits and benefits, the child disability benefit and other income-tested amounts are not included. These are planning estimates, not CRA’s determination. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope.
